html:
Mass protests in Hong Kong that began in 2019 against a bill to allow extradition to mainland China, and grew into a movement for democracy.

Many Hong Kongers feared the bill would expose them to China's courts and end the freedoms promised under One Country, Two Systems when Britain handed the city back in 1997. In June 2019 marchers filled the streets in numbers organisers put at up to two million. The chief executive, Carrie Lam, suspended the bill, then withdrew it in September, but the protests went on with five demands, including an inquiry into police violence and universal suffrage. Clashes grew fierce, with tear gas, petrol bombs and a siege at a university. In November pro-democracy candidates swept the district elections.

The COVID-19 pandemic ended mass gatherings. On 30 June 2020 Beijing imposed the National Security Law, and most opposition leaders were later jailed or fled. The movement followed the Umbrella Movement of 2014 and echoed the Tiananmen Square protests of 1989.
sum: Mass protests in Hong Kong that began in 2019 against a bill to allow extradition to mainland China, and grew into a movement for democracy.
